name: Reconciliation and Settlement
intent: Compare your own records of payments with the payment provider's and the bank's, match them by reference and by fallback rules, classify every difference, and route the unmatched ones to repair or review, so you always know where every cent is.
scenario: A shop recorded 200 payments in a week. The provider's settlement file lists nearly the same payments, but a payment made at 23:59 appears a day later, one payment is missing on each side, one arrives twice, two are reported net of the provider's fee, some have a different status, and a few lost their reference id on the way. The finance team needs to know which differences are harmless timing, which are errors, and how much money is at stake.
problem: Your database, the provider's report and the bank statement are three records of the same money, written by different systems at different times, and they will disagree. Some differences are only timing and fix themselves tomorrow, others are real: a payment that was charged but never recorded, a refund that exists in only one place, a duplicate delivery that would be paid twice. If nobody compares the records, mistakes sit unnoticed until a customer complains or an audit asks, and by then the trail is cold. If the comparison is too strict, people drown in false alarms, and if it is too loose it pairs the wrong payments and hides the errors.

howItWorks.title: Three views of the same money
howItWorks.text: Your own records say what you believe happened: orders, charges, refunds. The provider's records, usually a transaction or settlement report, say what it processed and what it will pay out, typically net of fees and in batches. The bank statement says what actually arrived, usually as one deposit per batch. Reconciliation compares them in pairs: your records against the provider's, and the provider's payout totals against the bank. A difference is not a bug in itself, it is a question.

howItWorks.title: Match by a reference, then by fallback rules
howItWorks.text: The best key is a reference both sides carry, such as the payment id you sent or the provider's id that you stored. Matching by that id is exact and cheap. When an id is missing, a fallback can pair rows by amount and a date within a window, which is weaker: two different payments of the same amount on nearby days look the same. Each rule is a trade between missing real matches and creating false ones, so rules run in order, strictest first, and everything left goes to the exception list.

howItWorks.title: Know the kinds of break
howItWorks.text: Timing: the provider books a payment at a different time or in a different time zone, so it falls on the next day and fixes itself. Missing on one side: you charged and never recorded, or recorded and never charged. Duplicate: the same payment was delivered or recorded twice. Amount differs: fees, currency conversion or partial amounts, so a payout is lower than the sum of payments, and the fee has to be accounted for explicitly. Status differs: refunded here and captured there. Classifying a break tells you who has to act.

howItWorks.title: Route exceptions: repair or review
howItWorks.text: Each class has a destination. Timing breaks are re-checked after the window and cleared if they match. Safe, mechanical differences, such as a duplicate with the same id, can be repaired by a script that is idempotent. Everything else, such as a payment missing from your records or a status that disagrees, goes to a person with both rows side by side and the amount at stake. Keeping the money total of the open exceptions, not only the count, shows what matters first.

howItWorks.title: Run it every day and keep the history
howItWorks.text: The comparison runs on a schedule, on a fixed cut-off, and stores its result: what matched, what was an exception, who resolved it and how. An exception that stays open for several days is more serious than a new one. The totals also close the loop: your matched payments, minus fees, should equal the provider's payout, and the payout should equal the deposit on the bank statement. If one of those totals does not tie, there is an error somewhere in the chain, even if every row matched.

pros: Finds missing, duplicated and wrongly recorded payments within a day instead of at the audit
Classification tells each team what to fix, and the money total shows what matters first
A fixed daily process and its stored history give auditors and partners evidence
Totals that tie out (payments, fees, payout, bank deposit) show that nothing is lost between the stages
cons: Needs a reliable reference id on every record, in both systems, and data in files or APIs you must parse
Fallback matching creates false matches that look like successes, which is worse than an honest unmatched row
Exception queues need people, and a flood of timing noise teaches them to ignore the list
Provider formats, cut-off times and time zones change, so the job needs maintenance and tests
whenToUse: Any business that takes payments through a provider and must account for every cent
Marketplaces and platforms that hold or pay out money to others
Systems where a charge, a refund or a payout can happen outside your own request flow, such as a webhook or a dispute
whenNotToUse: A single payment processed in the same database transaction as the record, with no outside system to compare
Data where small differences are expected and harmless, such as a rough analytics count
A fuzzy fix for missing ids when the real fix is to send and store a reference on every payment
pitfalls: Counting matched rows as correct without comparing amount, date and status, so a wrong amount hides behind a matching id
Loosening the fuzzy rule until the exception list looks short, and pairing different payments that happen to have the same amount
Ignoring time zones and cut-off times, so every payment near midnight is a break
Comparing gross payments with a net payout without accounting for fees, so the totals never tie
Auto-repairing differences without a record of what was changed and by whom
Reconciling only your records against the provider's and never the provider's payouts against the bank

roles.label: Your records
roles.description: Orders, charges and refunds as your own database believes them to be.

roles.label: Payment provider
roles.description: Publishes transaction and settlement reports and pays out in batches, net of fees.

roles.label: Bank statement
roles.description: Shows the deposits that actually arrived, usually one per batch.

roles.label: Reconciliation job
roles.description: Matches the records, classifies the differences and sends the unmatched on.

roles.label: Finance analyst
roles.description: Reviews the exceptions that no rule can repair.

quiz.question: A customer paid at 23:59 on Monday. Your records show Monday, and the provider's report lists the payment on Tuesday. The ids are the same. How should reconciliation treat it?
options: As an error to be corrected, by changing your record to Tuesday.
As a missing payment on both days, to be sent to review.
As a duplicate, because the same id appears on two different days.
As a timing difference: match on the id with a date window, and flag it only if it stays unmatched after the window.
quiz.explanation: The payment exists on both sides, and only the booking day differs, which is typical near midnight or across time zones. A date window lets the id match absorb it. Rewriting your record would lose the real time, and it is neither missing nor duplicated.

quiz.question: Some provider rows have lost their reference id, so the job pairs them with your rows by amount and a date within one day. What is the main risk of that rule?
options: Two different payments with the same amount around the same date can be paired, which hides both errors.
It is slower than matching by id, so the daily job will not finish.
It matches only payments that have a reference id, so it finds nothing.
It changes the amounts in your records to equal the provider's.
quiz.explanation: Amount and date are weak keys: many payments share them, so a pair can be wrong while looking like a success, and the real errors disappear from the exception list. Matching never edits records. Keep such rules last, count their pairs separately and fix the missing reference at its source.

quiz.question: The ids match, but the provider's report shows each payment a few percent lower than your records. What is the most likely cause, and the right way to handle it?
options: Your amounts are wrong, so reduce each recorded payment by the same percentage.
The provider reports payments net of its fee, so record the fee as its own line and match with that explained difference.
The provider lost part of each payment, so ask for the difference back.
The rounding of the cents differs, so round both sides to whole dollars before matching.
quiz.explanation: Providers typically deduct fees before paying out, so the report is net. The fee should be recorded explicitly, so that gross payments minus fees equal the payout. Editing the payments, or rounding both sides, throws away exactly the detail reconciliation exists to check.
